#1249. What's wrong with Erling Haaland? Man City's superstar has been radiating an air of gloom in front of the cameras - but it's his form on the pitch that should most concern Enzo Maresca, writes JACK GAUGHAN

Published: 08:22 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 12:10 EST, 25 November 2026

A smile did eventually spread across the face of Erling Haaland when dissecting Manchester City’s draw with Napoli, stretching their worrying run to one victory in five games.

Not for the first time in recent weeks, he had appeared morose and despondent, radiating an air of gloom, talking about how the team are ‘questioning anything’ amid these results. That’s not exactly inspiring confidence among their supporters.

But just as City’s captain for the night was about to finish his media duties before heading home, one final question focused on Sunday’s clash with Arsenal and a rivalry with a ‘certain centre half’. Haaland’s mood changed instantly.

‘It's always good to play against the best teams,’ said the Norwegian, breaking out into a smirk as he allowed the impending battle with Gabriel to percolate.

‘Arsenal were the best team last year and one of the best in the last five years now, so it's fun to play against them and it’s always fun to play against Gabriel.’

There was, at last, some positive emotion. Is Gabriel and that playground scrapping what he needs to re-energise? We’ll find out in a few days.

Erling Haaland appeared morose and despondent following Man City's draw with Napoli, suggesting he was 'questioning everything' amid their worrying run of form

Haaland did raise a smile about the prospect of his impending battle with Arsenal defender Gabriel this weekend

The Man City star has shown increasing dejected body language during games and has spent too much time recently with his head bowed and hand waving at team-mates

Haaland talked about City needing to be at their maximum to take anything from the Emirates this weekend. Whether that is ‘fun’ or not is a different matter entirely, but what Enzo Maresca must demand more from all of his players. Even with 14 goals already this term, that includes Haaland.

He is leading from the front off the pitch. Standing in front of the cameras more than anyone else, facing up to the dipping form and taking on those responsibilities without complaining. The forward wrote on X on Wednesday afternoon: 'Together through the ups and downs. Thank you for pushing us until the very end yesterday. Full focus on Sunday now.'

Yet City need more of that leadership between the white lines from somebody who has drawn a blank in four of his last five club matches, despite scoring three times over the international break.

There is too much head bowing and hand waving at the moment.

The 26-year-old admits he has to give extra. And believes that the team are generally creating enough chances for him, even if the freewheeling attacking abandon of early season has vanished.

City's results are clearly affecting Haaland’s mood and that can be self-perpetuating. He admits that failing to reverse this run is hurting him. That is evident by watching his increasingly dejected body language during games and the frustration seen when he gestured at Abdukodir Khusanov as the defender dithered with a routine throw-in during Saturday’s draw against Fulham. It wasn’t the picture of a man happy with his lot.

Only Haaland will know whether that general angst is contributing to a lack of intensity in his own performances. Nobody has mentioned the striker carrying a knock, although Maresca has appeared focused on offering him rest whenever possible over the past three months.

Something is undoubtedly proving an obstacle for him. He’s insisted that it isn’t the guilty verdicts hanging over City and, listening to him, the gripes and disappointment look focused on City’s lack of control in games. It also cannot help that Haaland will feel aggrieved to have seen a goal on Saturday chalked off for a foul on Bernd Leno and then to have not been awarded a penalty for grappling on Tuesday night.

If both or even one of those decisions go his way, the interview that sparked concern with fans – one conducted almost immediately after full time when emotions are at their highest – would likely have been very different.

City will have to cling on to the idea that a sullen Haaland is at least a Haaland who cares. And a Haaland who cares must surely dig them out of this hole, even if he cannot do that alone.

Iceland goalkeeper Ingvar Jonsson, who was in the famous Euro 2016 squad, has passed away at the age of just 37.

Back in the summer of 2016, Iceland surprised the football world as they managed to reach the quarter-finals of Euro 2016, which was held in France.

In the round of 16, Iceland were up against an England team packed with quality players, but pulled off a famous 2-1 win, with Ragnar Sigurdsson and Kolbeinn Sigthorsson scoring to cancel out Wayne Rooney’s opener.

At the time, Jonsson was an unused substitute as Iceland were eventually knocked out 5-2 by France, who then fell to a 1-0 defeat in the final against Cristiano Ronaldo’s Portugal. During the tournament, Iceland were also remembered for their fans' spectacular thunder clap celebration at the end of matches.

According to The Sun, Jonsson was diagnosed with cancer earlier in the year and sadly lost the battle this week, leaving behind his wife and three children.

On Thursday evening, Jonsson’s club, Vikingur Reykjavik, confirmed the 37-year-old’s death in a statement.

“It is with great sadness and deep sorrow that we announce that our dear friend and teammate Ingvar Jonsson, Víkingur’s goalkeeper, passed away on Wednesday, November 25, surrounded by his loved ones.

“The thoughts of the club and all Víkingur are with his family and loved ones. We send them our deepest condolences.”

Born in Keflavik, Jonsson began his football career at Njarovík, a club based in the Reykjanesbaer region of Iceland.

In 2011, Jonsson signed for Stjarnan, going on to win the Icelandic title for the first time in the club’s history; they did so by going the entire season without tasting defeat.

An official release from the police has been issued following the incident.

During what was a brilliant title-winning season in 2014, Jonsson played a huge role and was eventually voted as the Players’ Player of the Year.

As a result of his domestic success, Jonsson has also played in the Europa League and the Europa Conference League, with Stjarnan beating the likes of Motherwell and Lech Poznan before losing to Inter Milan in 2014.

After leaving Stjarnan ahead of the 2015-2016 campaign, he went on to play for IK Start, Sandnes Ulf, Sandefjord and Viborg before rounding off his career at Vikingur Reykjavik.

On the international stage, Jonsson earned eight caps for Iceland, having previously played for the U19s and the U21s. His senior team debut came in November 2014, when he replaced Ogmundur Kristinsson against Belgium.

#1245. Celtic's European opponents are plankton in football's great ocean... but Portuguese second-tier strugglers Torreense have already made waves in Europe this season

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 12:29 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 12:33 EST, 25 November 2026

Even for aficionados of the continental game, the draw for the Europa League this year was likely to cause a degree of puzzlement.

While not the only outfit to be making its debut in one of UEFA’s competitions, the name of S.C.U. Torreense rang precious few bells among supporters of clubs with a vested interest in how the cards might fall. And little wonder.

The Portuguese side are plankton in football’s great ocean. Not only have they never played on this stage before, they haven’t even come close to it.

An extraordinary triumph in the Portuguese Cup final – the Taca de Portugal – against Sporting Lisbon in May was their ticket to this journey. In all likelihood, this European adventure will be their first and their last.

It is, of course, not the done thing for anyone connected with any particular club to express a preference as to who they might be drawn against. But representatives of any one of the 35 other sides present at the Grimaldi Forum in Monaco in late August who claimed they weren’t privately hoping for a match against the men from the small city of Torres Vedras were lying.

Never mind Benfica, Porto and Sporting Lisbon, the traditional footballing powerhouses of that nation. In terms of support, stature and history, this outfit are a world removed from the likes of Braga and Vitoria Guimaraes, the perennial challengers to the big three.

Torreense players celebrate their victory over Armenian side Ararat in their last European tie

Torreense’s place in the food chain is underscored by the fact that they can’t even play European matches in their 2,400-capacity Estadio Manuel Marques home because it doesn’t match UEFA criteria.

For the purposes of the Europa League, their fans, who primarily hail from a place which sits 25 miles north of Lisbon, will have to travel to Leiria, which is 60 miles north of their home.

Those looking to pick up a late ticket for the visit of Celtic should have no concerns. Built for Euro 2004, the Estadio Municipal de Leiria holds 23,888 spectators. Torreense, who were a tier three side as recently as 2022, draw an average crowd of around 1,300.

The fact is that it’s not only a second division Portuguese side which Martin O’Neill’s men will face on matchday five. It’s a struggling one.

After ten matches in Liga Portugal 2, Joao Nuno’s men lie 13th of 18, 31st place overall in Portugal. They’ve won just twice this season, against Amarante and Benfica B, and have already had their cup defence ended by Benfica’s big boys.

Nuno was only appointed at the end of October after Luis Tralhao, who lifted the only major honour in the club’s history, was fired after a dismal start.

Portuguese coach Joao Nuno only took charge at the struggling second-tier side this season

Yet the concern for O’Neill and his players is that the Torreense which routinely fails to impress in its domestic division bears little resemblance to the one which has so far pitched up on its maiden European adventure.

In one of the most eye-catching results of the opening night, the Portuguese minnows travelled to Norway and defeated Lillestrom, a respected name throughout Europe, 2-1.

Sunderland were the first visitors to Leiria in October. What a game Torreense gave the Premier League side, leading by a goal only to narrowly lose the match late on.

While a 4-1 loss to Celtic’s old foes Ferencvaros in Budapest was something of a reality check, Nuno’s players fought back from a goal down to beat Ararat-Armenia in injury time last time out at their adopted home.

So, despite being wretched in their own league, they have six points in the Europa League and presently sit in 19th place, above the likes of Real Sociedad, AC Milan and Marseille.

With nine points possibly being enough to squeeze through to the play-off round, a famous win against Celtic could do the trick with three games to spare. With around £400,000 earned in prize money for any victory, you’d better believe they’ll be up for this.

Having just about lived to tell the tale last month, Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris gave Celtic a warning about what lies in store on Thursday.

Despite their lowly status, Torreense are above AC Milan, Celtic and Marseille in the table

‘It’s a good team they know how to manage this kind of game,’ said the Frenchman. ‘They’re well organised and hard to break down with this deep block. They try to seize every opportunity.’

A limited side which sits in and plays with caution? Those Celtic supporters who had the misfortune to watch their favourites fail to break down an atrocious Kairat Almaty outfit across 210 minutes little over a year ago will be rightly concerned.

While the Parkhead men’s poor record on the road across many years includes some thumpings at the hands of super clubs including Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain, there have been enough stumbles against lesser sides to ensure nothing can be taken for granted.

O’Neill will point to the displays in last season’s victories away to Feyenoord and Stuttgart as examples of what he’s looking for. While not on his watch, the catastrophe away to Kairat remains a useful illustration of what may happen if the players aren’t at it.

With an early goal likely to kick the legs from under Torreense, Celtic cannot allow them to feel comfortable in their shape.

In order to disrupt the Portuguese, it will be a night for the visitors to play with speed and imagination. To get in behind their defence, O’Neill’s wingers need to shine.

Sunderland required a late goal from Noah Sadiki to emerge with a victory on their trip to Leiria

This will have informed the veteran’s thinking as he sought to draft in a replacement for the injured Mika Baur.

While bringing in Joel van den Berg would have made sense from a positional point of view, Jota has started to show signs that he’s moving through the levels after a year-and-a-half out injured. A goal or an assist on his return to his homeland would allow the former Benfica man to underscore that point.

A constant threat against St Mirren, Yang Hyun-jun should start on the right flank ahead of Haissem Hassan. Together with Seb Tounekti, the Egyptian increasingly feels like a peripheral player.

Even if Benjamin Nygren is available again after a heel injury, O’Neill will be loath to drop Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain or Luke McCowan after both showed up well when played alongside Callum McGregor in the weekend win.

The issue of Kasper Hogh’s 16-game goal drought will only become pertinent if the free-scoring Camilo Duran can first help to put the game to bed.

Fit-again winger Jota could feature for Celtic on his return to Portuguese soil

Celtic badly need this to be a rare straightforward evening on the road in Europe. Goodness knows, they’ve had precious few of those in recent times.

A win to go with the one they claimed last time out against Besiktas would leave them in a decent position in the competition, with a further four points from their remaining matches with Omonia, Marseille and Union Saint-Gilloise then assuring them of progression.

Anything other than that outcome tonight doesn’t bear thinking about. Almost 60 years on from Jock Stein’s side becoming sporting immortals by defeating Inter Milan in Lisbon, their successors must tick a box and ensure tiny Torreense’s reputation in the game remains as lowly as it has ever been.

#1244. Carrick weighs up stripping Bruno Fernandes of Man Utd captaincy

A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

United are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

Pressed on whether Fernandes’s comments were all the more insidious and divisive at a time when the manager was trying to pull the squad together so soon after Martínez’s outburst, Carrick added: “Yeah, the most important thing for me is the team.

“First and foremost is the squad, the dynamics in the squad. And again, it’s about the club. And I’ll always do what’s best for the club.”

Carrick, Wilcox and United chief executive Omar Berrada held a meeting with Martínez in the wake of his criticism but the manager would not be drawn on whether he had spoken with Fernandes and it remains to be seen if he will be captain or start against Bournemouth.

“If I’ve spoken to him or haven’t spoken to him, I don’t think this is the time to go into too much detail,” he said.

Carrick agreed that United collectively needed to stop turning on each other in public. “We need to move forward in the right direction. We need to do things that enable us to do that. That’s pretty clear,” he said.

“It [the dressing room] is not divided, no. We just need to get back to doing what we do best and we will.”

Separately, Carrick expressed sympathy for Fernandes over the “awful” burglary at his home on Wednesday night when he was in Italy, and said the club “are doing a lot of work to support Bruno and his family”.

Carrick is under huge pressure heading into Bournemouth but said he was happy to take the heat if it enabled his players to perform.

“It is my responsibility whatever goes on the pitch, and what we are as a group, and what we look like, and what we feel like,” he said. “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry.”

Nonetheless, Carrick admitted he was “hurting an awful lot” and that the team had to get back to showing the values and qualities that have underpinned the club’s historic success after a “really unacceptable” performance against Como and wider struggles. United have won two of 11 matches this season.

“I’m not entitled to be here,” Carrick said. “We’re not entitled to win. We’ve won in the past, we’ve got an incredible history, but that doesn’t mean you’re entitled to just win.

“I’m fully aware of that. It takes hard work, a lot of sacrifice. You’ve got to invest yourself in the club and you’ve got to do a lot of things that maybe aren’t so nice, but you’ve got to do it for each other, and you’ve got to win.

“It’s important we live up to that, and it’s important for me to push those values, and for our supporters to feel that moving forward.

“We’ve kind of lost our way a bit if I’m honest, and we will get it back. I’m totally confident we’ll get it back. Respect this club, respect what it takes, because it’s very important to me.”

Carrick added that he was inspired by the values of “humility, hard work, resilience, sacrifice and pride” embodied by the likes of Busby, Ferguson, Charlton, Giggs and Rooney.

“We can never lose that, and I won’t let us lose that,” he said. “We’ve had it for a spell, I feel very strongly about that. It inspires me a lot to live up to that and keep driving that with the players.

“There’s a resilience about this club that’s been shown for a long time. Whether that’s bouncing back from adversity, comebacks, late goals, success, sustaining success, there’s a resilience in this club that runs very deep.”

Carrick was trailed by a camera crew from Amazon Prime as he entered the media auditorium at Manchester United’s Carrington training base at 1.30pm on Friday.

There have been plenty of dark moments at Old Trafford in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era. But the difference this season is that any internal drama will soon be available for public consumption after the decision to allow cameras into a once-sacrosanct dressing room.

Whether Carrick will see out the next week, let alone a season being captured by filmmakers from Amazon’s All Or Nothing series, who probably cannot believe their luck at the unfolding crisis, remains to be seen. He certainly needs a big reaction against Bournemouth at Old Trafford at the very least.

But it became clear as he began his press conference with an emotional 5½-minute monologue that he would not go down without a fight.

Sir Alex Ferguson is the best manager of all-time. The greatest, for me. And working for him, his main priority was Manchester United.

Sir Matt [Busby] and Sir Bobby [Charlton], their resilience was beyond belief what they showed and how they rebuilt this football club. It was based on being humble, having humility and hard work. We can never lose that and I won’t let us lose that.

We’ve lost our way if I’m totally honest but we’ll get back what it takes.

Carrick has come in, trailed by the Amazon cameras, sat down and made an address for five minutes before taking any questions. He acknowledges it’s not been good enough or what the club expects and that it’s got to get better. He’s talking about rebuilding this club based on humility, values and hard work and won’t let that go and that it inspires him going forward. “Yeah we’re in a moment where it’s not going well but we need to show exactly what it means and respect what it means to be here and what it takes to win,” he said. “You’re not entitled to win. It takes hard work.”

I think it’s important... recently we haven’t had a good time I think that’s obvious, I totally accept that.

We had five months of relative success and I was happy with many things I was seeing.

We haven’t done well enough recently. Wednesday was a bad night for a lot of reasons, it really hurt a lot, it hurt me to see how the game panned out.

As I said after the game, it was unacceptable.

Hopefully he will be in position by half-past, but it is not unlike managers to keep everyone waiting.

My name has been linked with numerous clubs, but there are currently no negotiations at an advanced stage.

Following a wonderful and successful spell in charge of Napoli, I will take the time I need to consider how and when to return to management. It will be a carefully considered decision, one I will make when I believe the conditions are right.

I have read reports of financial demands and requests for full control that I have supposedly already made to the clubs mentioned, as well as reservations about what has been described as my “strong personality”. These reports are unfounded, as there is currently no concrete basis for such assessments.

Should a concrete opportunity arise, that will be the time to hold discussions with the club concerned and jointly consider the terms of a potential agreement, with due regard for both parties’ needs and the qualities and approach that define my work as a manager.

Until then, any assumptions about my demands and my professional future remain speculation and cannot be treated as fact.

For all his brilliance and ruthlessness as a businessman, Sir Jim Ratcliffe has yet to convince that he has any feel for football. Just look at the performance of Ineos’s other prize assets this season: Lausanne-Sport lie 12th in the 12-team Swiss top flight after one win in 10, and Nice are a distant 13th in Ligue 1, having burnt through eight different managers during the petrochemical giant’s seven years in charge.

As James Ducker and Sam Dean explore in this piece, a succession of Manchester United managers have admonished their team for a lack of industry and athleticism. A number of factors may be to blame: recruitment errors, paralysing pressure and a bad dressing-room culture among them. It is time to get back to basics.

Michael Carrick is not one of the Premier League’s more loquacious managers but supporters will be interested in what he has to say at his pre-Bournemouth press conference this afternoon.

The Manchester United manager is under severe pressure after a run of no wins in seven games across all competitions, and senior players are talking out of school in post-game interviews.

Just when it appeared a line had been drawn under Lisandro Martinez taking on technical director Jason Wilcox, Bruno Fernandes reached for a petrol can and poured more fuel on the flames.

Speaking after the dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como, Fernandes called out Carrick and his coaching staff for their tactical approach, specifically a reluctance to press opponents aggressively in a man-to-man fashion.

Carrick, by his own very measured standards, delivered a pointed response.

“We actually were half-pressed man to man in the second half and then conceded a goal from that,” he said. “And there’s a little bit on whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win.”

Their opponents on Sunday are Bournemouth, who after a lean run of results under Marco Rose have just dispatched Sunderland for their first league victory of the season, and the mighty AC Milan in the Europa League.

Things do not get easier for United, who go to Stamford Bridge next weekend before a home game against Aston Villa before the November international break.

Telegraph Sport reported on Thursday that former Bayern Munich and Germany manager Julian Nagelsmann features prominently and is understood to want the job – as does Antonio Conte. United are also tracking Fabian Hurzeler while there is interest in Eddie Howe.

United are currently 13th in the table with seven points from seven games.

#1243. Tottenham Star Wants to Join Premier League Rivals in January

Tottenham forward Richarlison could be on his way out the door in the January transfer window, and he's keen on a move to a Premier League rival.

The Brazilian international hasn't featured for Spurs so far this season after he was left out of their Premier League squad for the campaign.

A departure in January now feels inevitable for Richarlison. He's clearly not wanted at Spurs and came close to leaving the club in the summer window.

Richarlison has only featured for the club's U21 side so far this season, and it makes sense for all parties if he moves on as soon as possible.

Spurs were still demanding a relative high fee for Richarlison during the summer transfer window, so it will be interesting to see whether they lower their asking price in the coming months.

According to a report from Sky Sports journalist Lyall Thomas, Everton haven't ruled out making another move to sign Richarlison in the January transfer window after attempting to secure his signature in the summer.

The report claims that other Premier League clubs are interested, while Turkish outfit Trabzonspor are also there for Richarlison.

Thomas claims that Richarlison would be open to making a move to Everton in January, but it will be interesting to see whether the two clubs can do a deal.

During the summer, a deal was taking place that would see Iliman Ndiaye go to Spurs, but the Senegalese international signed for Manchester City instead.

Everton likely won't want to include any players as part of a deal if they were to bring Richarlison back to Merseyside, but they certainly won't want to pay too much for a player on high wages who hasn't been playing.

The report claims that the key obstacle stopping Trabzonspor making a move is Spurs' valuation, with personal terms not expected to be a problem.

Will Williams-Barnett get the nod to start a second Premier League game in a row against Sunderland?

It certainly feels like it's time for Tottenham to move on from Richarlison.

The Brazilian's contract is set to expire next summer, and there's next to no chance that Spurs offer him a new deal.

Even just getting his wages off the books for the second half of the season would be beneficial, so Spurs need to find a way of getting rid of him in January.

A return to Everton could be a fairytale move for Richarlison, but it remains to be seen whether they can afford his wages or transfer fee.

A loan move where Everton pay a large portion of his salary could suit all parties, especially if interest doesn't ramp up ahead of January.

Liverpool have received a potentially significant injury boost after initial medical tests suggested Víctor Munoz has avoided a serious knee injury following Wednesday night’s 3-0 Champions League victory over Club Brugge.

Fears of a lengthy layoff initially surged at the Jan Breydelstadion when the 23-year-old collapsed in agony in the 42nd minute after colliding with Club Brugge defender Jorne Spileers following a blistering run into the penalty area.

Although a stretcher was called onto the pitch, Munoz was eventually able to limp off under his own power.

According to Spanish outlet Marca (as relayed by Tribuna), initial medical tests conducted back on Merseyside suggest Munoz has escaped structural ligament damage. Instead, the setback is believed to be a heavy impact knock.

Final confirmation pending as Liverpool hope for best news

While the early diagnostic feedback is hugely encouraging, final medical confirmation remains pending as club doctors continue monitoring how the joint responds once swelling subsides.

Even if it proves to be a severe bone bruise, Sunday’s Premier League Merseyside derby away against Everton may come slightly too soon.

Speaking during his post-match press conference in Belgium, head coach Andoni Iraola had already offered cautious optimism that the issue was not very serious. He said (via Liverpoolfc.com):

“He was with a lot of pain when he left the pitch. He was a lot more positive when the game had finished.

“It has been a knock on the knee, so now we have to assess him. Then if he presents well tomorrow and it’s just this knock… After the game, I talked to him and he was a little bit more optimistic.”

Signed from Osasuna for £34.5 million during the summer transfer window, Munoz is rapidly looking like one of the bargains of the season.

Fresh off finding the net in Sunday’s 4-0 demolition of Manchester United, his electric pace, direct dribbling, and relentless pressing has been vital to Iraola’s attack.

Munoz has scored three and assisted another in five starts this season across all competitions.

While Bradley Barcola and Rio Ngumoha may be ahead of Munoz in the pecking order at the moment, Andoni Iraola is doing a wnoderful job managing the squad, rotating the players across the various competitions.

Liverpool will hope that Munoz’s injury isn’t too serious and that he is back soon ahead of the busy run of fixtures in the coming month.

#1241. Engineering signalling centres to trigger human trunk morphogenesis in vitro

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Vertebrate trunk development is orchestrated by endogenous signalling centres that generate gradients of signals such as WNT and BMP to pattern cell fates and drive morphogenesis1,2,3,4,5,6,7. Whether these cues alone can reconstitute human trunk-like morphogenesis in vitro remains unknown. Here we present a synthetic embryology platform for high-throughput, spatiotemporal delivery of morphogen signals to epithelial cysts derived from human pluripotent stem cells. Transient WNT and BMP gradients are sufficient to drive the generation of axially elongating trunk-like structures that contain a central neural tube flanked by axial, paraxial, intermediate and lateral mesoderm. The geometry of the transient BMP signal exerts lasting control over mediolateral patterning and bilateral symmetry. Patterning and morphogenesis are sustained by neuromesodermal and lateral plate mesoderm progenitors induced by the initial cues, which act as endogenous signalling centres. Together, these findings define a minimal spatial code sufficient to reconstitute trunk-like morphogenesis in a human stem-cell-based model and establish a scalable platform for studying early human development and congenital disorders.

a, A detailed schematic of the workflow is shown: (i) Matrigel is microcontact printed onto the two-layered PDMS stamp (PDMS-ii) using a flat PDMS stamp (PDMS-i). (ii) A thin PDMS microwell array is peeled from the silicon master and overlaid on a glass coverslip. Taller PDMS sidewalls are plasma-bonded along two edges. (iii) Capillary water flow through the microchannels drives localized Matrigel transfer from stamp PDMS-ii onto the PDMS microwell layer at the contact interface. (iv) Cells are seeded onto the transferred Matrigel pattern, overlaid with a silanized coverslip atop the sidewalls, and cultured further with media and microwell-trapped beads. b, Photographs of the experimental setup corresponding to steps a(i–iii): coating the flat stamp (grey border, fourth column, top); PDMS-ii stamps with different patterns (blue border, first column); PDMS microwell layer with wells at different positions (red border, second column); aligned PDMS-ii stamp and PDMS microwell layer in contact (green border, third column); and the application of weight and water flow for transfer (green border, fourth column, bottom). MG, Matrigel; RT, room temperature.

a–d, Design of two-layer PDMS stamp and microwell substrate: a, upper-layer pattern used to print Matrigel features; b, lower-layer embedded microchannels (white denotes channel features); c, assembled two-layer PDMS stamp with a three-dimensional illustration of the assembled stamp below; d, alignment of stamp features and microwell layer, with 120 µm diameter microwells positioned at defined distances from pattern edges. Scale bars, 1 mm. e, Whole-chip images show humidified microcontact printing (HµCP) of Matrigel mixed with fluorescently conjugated BSA (cyan) onto PDMS microwell chip (brightfield, grey), using a four-square stamp pattern. Air bubbles beneath PDMS microwell layer and above glass coverslip are visible in brightfield images. Images are representative of 6 independent experiments (12 chips) with similar results. Scale bars, 1 mm. f, Whole-chip image shows standard microcontact printing (µCP) of fluorescent BSA onto glass to validate stamp pattern from a. Image is representative of 2 independent experiments (5 chips) with similar results. Scale bar, 1 mm. g, Image shows pluripotent epithelial cysts formed 3 days after seeding on a PDMS microwell chip, using stamp pattern from a. A diversity of cyst arrangements, rather than the optimized hexagonal pattern with a central cyst as in Fig. 1, are used to show the flexibility of the approach. Image is representative of 79 independent experiments (145 chips) with similar results. Scale bar, 1 mm. h, Whole-chip epifluorescence image shows pluripotent cysts (DAPI, grey), well-trapped BMP4-coated beads (pseudocoloured red), and pSMAD1/5/9 immunofluorescence (pSMAD, green) 6 h after bead deposition. Image is representative of 6 independent experiments (13 chips) with similar results. Scale bar, 1 mm. i, Representative higher magnification images of cyst arrays with adjacent BMP beads and pSMAD1/5/9 immunofluorescence 6 h after bead deposition, from three independent experiments. (Top row) Five-cyst arrays with one or two beads, from chip in h. (Bottom left) Seven-cyst array with two beads, from an independent experiment. (Bottom right) Five-cyst array with three beads, from an independent experiment. Scale bars, 100 µm. j, (Left) Plot shows normalized pSMAD1/5/9 intensity (pSMAD/DAPI) versus distance from BMP bead, d, for all cysts from chip in h except cysts at centre of arrays (n = 201 cysts; light grey lines, individual cyst profiles; solid lines, mean; shaded areas, ±1 s.d.). (Right) pSMAD1/5/9 intensity in the bead-proximal epithelium of each cyst is plotted against the distance to the nearest bead, dmin, showing a negative correlation (red line, R2 = 0.624; n = 156 cysts) up to a distance of 635 µm, beyond which the intensity is low and uncorrelated (R2 = 0.061; n = 45 cysts). k, (Left) Normalized pSMAD1/5/9 is plotted against angle relative to bead direction (θ - θb) for cysts within responsive regime (d < 635 µm; n = 156 cysts). (Right) The direction of the pSMAD1/5/9 distribution, quantified by its first moment, is plotted as a function of the angle towards the nearest bead, θb (R2 = 0.17, n = 156 cysts). The correlation between pSMAD1/5/9 direction and bead angle is weaker than in Fig. 1f due to the overlapping influence of multiple BMP beads positioned near most cyst arrays in h.

a, (top) Live YFP and merged Brightfield (BF)–YFP images show hexagonally arranged cysts derived from the BMP4-T2A-Achilles reporter hPSC line 6 h after exposure to BMP4-coated beads (pseudocoloured red), with no detectable YFP signal. Images are from one experiment (36 cyst arrays). (bottom) Live images of the cysts from (top) 24 h after bead exposure show the presence of YFP (arrowhead) in some cells adjacent to beads. Images are from one experiment (2 cyst arrays). b, Plot of BMP4 read counts per million (CPM) from bulk RNA sequencing of pluripotent cysts at 0 h, 7 h, and 24 h after BMP bead exposure (n = 3 biologically independent samples per timepoint). Dots, individual samples; bars, mean; error bars, ±1 s.d. BMP5 expression was not detected in any of the samples. c, (left) Brightfield, DAPI (grey) and definitive endoderm marker SOX17 immunofluorescence (cyan) images show spatially arranged cysts after a 2-day exposure to the main experimental conditions, including BMP bead exposure, WNT-driven symmetry breaking, and Activin/Nodal signalling inhibitor A83-01 (above), or without A83-01 (below). Images are from one experiment per condition (with A83-01: 1 chip, 21 cyst arrays; without A83-01: 2 chips, 47 cyst arrays). (right) Bulk RNA-seq analysis of key endodermal genes in cysts under the same two conditions, with (green, n = 3 biologically independent samples) or without A83-01 (purple, n = 2 biologically independent samples). Dots, individual samples; bars, mean; error bars, ±1 s.d. A83-01 prevents endoderm differentiation in all protocols here (Extended Data Fig. 5b, Fig. 4, Supplementary Data 5). d, (left) Plot of DAPI-normalized SOX2 and TBXT intensity versus distance from central cyst of array (“anterior”). TBXT varies more with distance from anterior than distance from bead (Fig. 2c) due to A–P symmetry breaking from geometric cyst arrangement16,17 (Fig. 1b). Black arrow indicates the regime where both TBXT and SOX2 are high, corresponding to NMP differentiation (n = 210 biologically independent cysts; thin lines, individual cyst profiles; thick line, mean; shaded area, 95% confidence interval). (right) Pixel density plot of normalized SOX2 versus TBXT; percentages, fractions of pixels above and below the cutoffs. 28% of pixels are SOX2+ TBXT+, indicative of NMP-like expression. e, Brightfield, DAPI (grey), and TBXT immunofluorescence (cyan) images of three hexagonal cyst arrays without (left) or with a central cyst (right) on the same chip. In the absence of the central cyst, hexagonal cysts are prone to express TBXT on both their inward- and outward-facing poles (white arrowheads), indicating a lack of clear A-P polarity. With the central cyst present, TBXT expression is restricted to the outward-facing pole. Images are representative of 2 independent experiments (12 cyst arrays) with similar results. f, Brightfield and immunofluorescence images of cysts after 2 days of differentiation show FOXF1+ nascent lateral plate mesoderm (LPM, red) proximal to BMP4-coated beads (pseudocoloured red; red arrows top left, white arrows elsewhere), whereas FOXA2+ anterior mesoderm (magenta) and SOX2+ neural progenitors (yellow) are distant from beads. Cysts are from another chip of the same design (Extended Data Fig. 2a). Images are representative of 3 independent experiments with similar results. g, Pixel-density plots of FOXA2 versus FOXF1 (top) and SOX2 versus FOXF1 (bottom) immunofluorescence in day 2 cysts, indicating mutual exclusivity. Colour, log-scaled pixel density normalized to the 99th percentile of bin density; contours, equally spaced iso-density lines; dashed lines, positivity thresholds; percentages, fraction of pixels in each quadrant. n = 7 biologically independent cysts from 3 independent experiments. h, Images of cysts after 2 days of differentiation show FOXF1+ nascent LPM located proximally to BMP beads, FOXA2+ anterior mesoderm distant from beads, and TBXT+ mesoderm at posterior end of cysts. Images are representative of 5 independent experiments with similar results. i, Per-chip fraction of cysts containing FOXF1:Achilles+ cells, plotted as in Fig. 2e, for each condition: adjacent to a BMP bead (“Bead”), no bead (“No Bead”) and adjacent to a bead following BMPR1A knockdown (“KD”). Dots, one chip from each of four independent experiments; bars, mean; error bars, ±1 s.d. across experiments. n = 182 (“Bead”), 1,010 (“No Bead”) and 189 (“KD”) cysts scored in total (see Methods, “Fraction of FOXF1+ cysts”). j, BMPR1A CPM from bulk RNA-seq of cells following BMPR1A knockdown compared with a scrambled control (n = 3 biologically independent samples per condition). Dots, individual samples; bars, mean; error bars, ±1 s.d. Two-sided Welch’s t-test: t = −7.00, d.f. = 2.5, P = 0.010, mean difference −28.1 CPM (95% CI, −42.3 to −13.9). *P < 0.05. k, Quantification of pSMAD1/5/9 in cells at the edge following 30 min treatment with 10 ng ml−1 BMP4. BMPR1A knockdown cells show reduced pSMAD1/5/9 compared with SCRAMBLE control cells (n = 3 biologically independent samples per condition). Additional quantification at different time points and cell locations is provided in Supplementary Data 4. Dots, per-well medians; centre line, median; boxes, interquartile range; whiskers, extreme values within 1.5× interquartile range. l, Representative immunostaining images for the analysis in k: BMPR1A knockdown (top row) and SCRAMBLE (bottom row); knockdown cells (CFP, yellow, left), DAPI (middle), and pSMAD1/5/9 (cyan, right). Images are from one experiment (3 wells each). m, Images show two additional replicates of day 2 morphs as in Fig. 2f, showing the co-expression of BMP4:Achilles (green) and FOXF1:mScarlet3 (red). Images are representative of 3 independent experiments (13 chips) with similar results. n, Fluorescent RNA in situ hybridization images for BMP4 (green) and FOXF1 (red) transcripts show co-localization in a bead-adjacent cyst after 2 days of differentiation. Representative image from n = 6 biologically independent bead-adjacent cysts. o, Pixel-density plot of FOXF1 versus BMP4 in situ signal in the day 2 cyst shown in n. Colour, log-scaled pixel density normalized to its maximum; contours, equally spaced iso-density lines. The two signals are positively correlated (R2 = 0.646). Scale bars, 100 µm.

a, A schematic of trunk morph differentiation protocol is shown. hPSCs were seeded onto micropatterned PDMS microwell substrate on Day −3 in mTeSR Plus with 10 µM Y-27632. The next day, Y-27632 was removed from media conditions and Matrigel added to induce the formation of single lumen epithelial cysts. On Day 0, BMP4-coated beads were injected into microwells, and cyst differentiation was initiated in N2B27 with 8–10 µM CHIR99021, 0.1–0.15 µM A83-01, and 50 ng ml−1 NOGGIN. After 48 h, cysts were transferred to individual wells in N2B27 with Matrigel and cultured for 3–4 days before analysis. b, Box-and-whisker plots show length of trunk morphs at 0, 48, and 120 h of differentiation. The same n = 93 biologically independent trunk morph samples were tracked across all three time points. Centre line, median; boxes, 25th-75th percentile; whiskers, 1.5 × the interquartile range beyond the quartiles; dots, individual trunk morphs. c, (left) Box-and-whisker plots of trunk morph length on days 3, 4 and 5 without (red, n = 10 biologically independent trunk morph samples) or with the WNT-secretion inhibitor IWP3 (green, n = 8 biologically independent trunk morph samples), added after 48 h; each morph was tracked across all three time points. Centre line, median; boxes, 25th-75th percentile; whiskers, 1.5 × the interquartile range beyond the quartiles; dots, individual trunk morphs. Differences between conditions at each time point were assessed using two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons; Hodges-Lehmann median differences are given with Bonferroni-adjusted (98.3%) confidence intervals. Day 3: U = 16, P = 0.103, −59 µm (−160 to 18). Day 4: U = 4, P = 1.6 × 10−3, −212 µm (−314 to −100). Day 5: U = 0, P = 1.4 × 10−4, −353 µm (−438 to −287). ns, P > 0.05; **, P < 0.01; ***, P < 0.001. (Right) Fluorescent RNA in situ hybridization images for WNT3A (left, green) and WNT5A (right, magenta) transcripts, together with brightfield imaging, show WNT ligand expression at the posterior end (n = 5 biologically independent trunk morph samples per probe, from 2 independent experiments). d, Representative epifluorescence images of trunk morphs after transient BMP4-bead exposure show FOXF1+ lateral plate mesoderm (cyan) bilaterally (left), unilaterally (middle), and posteriorly localized (right). Images are representative of 3 independent experiments (11 chips, 93 trunk morphs scored across all bead configurations) with similar results. e, Representative images of day 5 trunk morphs following transient exposure to medially positioned BMP4-coated beads. Posterior-restricted LPM was observed only at bead-cyst distances below 160 µm (5 of 12 morphs); all 9 trunk morphs with larger distances showed bilateral FOXF1. Images are from one experiment (3 chips, 21 trunk morphs). f-g, Representative images of trunk morphs exposed to (f) a unilateral bead or (g) two bilateral beads show unilateral or bilateral FOXF1, respectively. MESP2:mCherry is bilateral in all morphs. Images are representative of the same experiments and morphs as in d. h, Confocal images show DAPI (grey), MESP2:mCherry (red), phalloidin (grey), and FOXF1 (cyan) in a trunk morph. Single lumen, polarized somites (white arrows) are visible within the single focal plane. Images are representative of 2 independent experiments (2 trunk morphs) with similar results. i, Confocal images show DAPI (grey), phalloidin (grey), FOXC1 (cyan), and MESP2:mCherry (red) in a trunk morph. Single lumen, polarized somites (white arrows) are visible within the single focal plane. Images are representative of 2 independent experiments (4 trunk morphs) with similar results. j, Confocal images show DAPI (grey), phalloidin (grey), PAX3 (red), and SOX2 (yellow) in a trunk morph. Single lumen, polarized somites (white arrows) are visible in a 30-µm z-projection. Images are representative of 3 independent experiments (7 trunk morphs) with similar results. k, Confocal images at different z-planes (z = 330, 380, and 745 µm from the base) of trunk morph in Fig. 3h show DAPI (grey), FOXF1 (cyan), and MESP2:mCherry (red). As in many trunk morphs, somites (white arrows) are visible at specific confocal planes but are not apparent in the maximum z-projection shown in Fig. 3h. Scale bar, 100 µm.

a, Confocal images of day 5 trunk morphs with medial bead (left) or unilateral bead exposure (right) show DAPI (grey), MESP2:mCherry (red; paraxial mesoderm), PAX8 (yellow; intermediate mesoderm), and FOXF1:Achilles (cyan; LPM), along with inset images of lateral region at higher magnification. Images are representative of 10 independent experiments (55 trunk morphs) with similar results. b, Epifluorescence images of day 5 trunk morphs without beads (left, three morphs; brightfield) or with a medial bead (right; DAPI, grey) show MESP2:mCherry (red; paraxial mesoderm), FOXA2 (green; axial mesoderm) and no SOX17 (magenta; endoderm). FOXA2+ cells are present in all morphs but fewer in morphs exposed to bead. Yellow outlines mark the boundary to which images were cropped for display (see Methods, “Image display”). Images are representative of 2 independent experiments (3 chips) with similar results. c, Epifluorescence (left, right) and confocal (middle) images of day 5 trunk morphs exposed to BMP4-coated beads in three configurations: medial (left), unilateral (middle), and bilateral (right). FOXF1 (cyan) appears unilaterally or bilaterally reflecting bead geometry, whereas MESP2:mCherry (red) is bilateral in all conditions. FOXA2 is confined to medial regions and diminished relative to no-bead controls in b. Images are representative of 8 independent experiments with similar results. Scale bars, 100 µm.

a, Hierarchically clustered single-cell gene expression matrices of stem cell-based trunk morphs after 6 days of differentiation, without and with BMP bead exposure, are shown. Each column represents an individual cell, rows correspond to key genes, and matrix values show normalized gene expression as indicated by the colour scale. Cluster annotations are indicated by the colour bar and legend (right). n = 2,748 cells without beads; 2,558 cells with beads. b, UMAP plots of single-cell transcriptomes from day 6 trunk morphs are shown as in Fig. 4b, coloured by BMP bead exposure history (left) and by cluster identity (right). c, Ordered list of gene panel used in a and in Fig. 4d,e. Genes were manually chosen and assigned as cluster-representative by comparing differentially expressed genes against established cell type markers from literature. d, Hierarchically clustered single-cell gene expression matrices from trunk morphs, without and with BMP bead exposure, are shown. Rows correspond to top five differentially expressed genes for each cluster as identified by multinomial logistic regression analysis.

a, (Left) Hierarchically subclustered single-cell gene expression matrices are shown for cells originally assigned to somite clusters (“Early Somite”, “Mature Somite”) from trunk morphs without and with BMP bead exposure (see Supplementary Data 1, 5). Each column represents an individual cell, rows correspond to differentially expressed genes with key genes bolded, and matrix values show internally normalized gene expression. Sub-cluster annotations are indicated by colour bar and legend below. n = 825 cells without beads; n = 129 cells with beads. (Top right) UMAP plots of 954 somite cell transcriptomes from trunk morphs without or with BMP bead exposure are shown, coloured by subcluster identity. (Bottom right) Stacked bar graphs show the fraction of each somite subcluster among somite cells from trunk morphs, without and with BMP bead exposure. b, Same as a, but for hierarchical subclustering of “Forebrain/Midbrain” cluster. n = 283 cells without beads; n = 263 cells with beads. c, Same as a but for cells from LPM and intermediate mesoderm (IM) clusters from BMP bead–exposed trunk morphs, revealing three distinct subpopulations: endothelial progenitors, cardiac-biased anterior trunk LPM, and posterior trunk LPM. Rows correspond to key differentially expressed marker genes. d, (Top) Images show brightfield, MESP2:mCherry (red), and FOXF1:Achilles (YFP, cyan) in a live day 8 trunk morph pre-fixation. (Bottom) Images show the same morph after fixation and fluorescent RNA in situ hybridization for hindlimb marker TBX4 (yellow). Note that HCR processing shrinks morphs and reduces reporter signals. Images are from one experiment (3 trunk morphs). e, Hierarchically subclustered gene expression matrix separates floor plate from notochord. Rows correspond to key differentially expressed marker genes. f, Hierarchically subclustered gene expression matrix of roof plate (RP) and neural crest (NC) cluster cells from BMP bead–exposed trunk morphs shows eight distinct subpopulations: dorsal neuron progenitors, roof plate epithelium, neural crest progenitors, pre-migratory neural crest, early migratory neural crest, migratory cranial neural crest, neural crest–derived neural progenitors, and neural crest–derived immature neurons. Rows correspond to key differentially expressed marker genes. g, Epifluorescence images of a day 6 trunk morph show DAPI (grey), SOX2 (cyan; neural tube), PAX3 (magenta; dorsal neural tube and somites), BMP4:Achilles (green), and FOXF1:mScarlet3 (blue; LPM). The BMP4 and FOXF1 channels show reporter fluorescence; SOX2 and PAX3 are immunostains acquired in a second imaging round after quenching, aligned to the first round using DAPI (see Methods). BMP4 expression in the neural tube is faint compared to the mesoderm. Images are representative of 2 independent experiments (one trunk morph from each) with similar results. h, Epifluorescence images of a day 6 trunk morph differentiated with a BMP bead and treated with SHH agonist SAG starting on day 4, displaying DAPI (grey), SOX2 (cyan), PAX3 (magenta), FOXA2 (green; axial mesoderm and floor plate of neural tube), MESP2 (red), and FOXF1 (blue). The MESP2 and FOXF1 channels show reporter fluorescence; SOX2, PAX3 and FOXA2 are immunostains acquired in a second imaging round after quenching, aligned to the first round using DAPI (see Methods). PAX3 and FOXA2 expression demonstrate dorsoventral patterning of the neural tube. Images are representative of 2 independent experiments (4 chips, 6 trunk morphs) with similar results. Scale bar, 100 μm.

a, (Left) UMAP plot of single-cell transcriptomes from a week 3 human embryo (“W3-1 Embryo”), a week 4 human embryo (“W4-1 Embryo”), and a week 4 human embryonic head (“W4-2 Head”) is shown, coloured by hierarchical cluster. Corresponding annotations for the 50 clusters are shown on the plot (raw data from Zeng et al.29). (Right) Same UMAP plot with cells coloured by embryo of origin. b, Stacked bar graphs show the fraction of cells in each cluster that originated from each embryo. c, Hierarchically clustered single-cell gene expression matrices of cells from the three human embryos are shown. Each column represents an individual cell, rows correspond to the top 10 differentially expressed genes for each cluster as identified by multinomial logistic regression, with key genes labelled, and matrix values show normalized gene expression. Cluster annotations are indicated by the colour bar corresponding to annotations in a and b. n = 46,768 cells. Abbreviations defined in Supplementary Data 2.

a, Single-cell gene expression matrix of individual cells from trunk morphs is shown as in Fig. 4f, with rows corresponding to known morphogen genes. Cluster annotations are indicated by colour bar and labels below. b, Gene expression violin plots of BMP receptor genes are shown for trunk morphs cells from each cluster. The width of the plot reflects the distribution of gene expression among cells as determined by kernel density estimation, and the colour of the plot corresponds to the median gene expression as shown in the legend on the right.

a, Confocal images of day 5 trunk morph transduced with a non-targeting scramble control sgRNA (yellow; CFP) for CRISPRi knockdown show DAPI (grey), MESP2:mCherry (red; paraxial mesoderm), and FOXF1 (cyan; LPM). Images are representative of 4 independent experiments (60 trunk morphs) with similar results. b, Confocal images of a mosaic day 5 trunk morph, in which 10% of cells are transduced with scramble construct and 90% are unmodified, show DAPI, MESP2:mCherry, and FOXF1 as in a. CFP+ scramble control knockdown cells are present within FOXF1+ LPM domain. Images are representative of 4 independent experiments (14 trunk morphs) with similar results. c, Live time series images of three trunk morphs at 48, 72, 96 and 116.25 h, generated from the BMP4-T2A-Achilles; FOXF1-T2A-mScarlet3 reporter hPSC line. Brightfield, mScarlet, and Achilles images show increasingly large and overlapping domains of BMP4 and FOXF1 reporter expression. Images are from one experiment (6 chips, 65 trunk morphs). d, Pixel density map of BMP4:Achilles versus FOXF1:mScarlet3 reporter intensity in time series images of trunk morphs from 48–116.25 h show that the majority of pixels are either FOXF1− BMP4− (lower left quadrant, 44.6%), FOXF1+ BMP4− (36%), or both FOXF1+BMP4+ (upper right quadrant, 18.3%), demonstrating that BMP4 expression is contained within a domain of FOXF1 expression (n = 59 of the 65 trunk morphs in c). e, Epifluorescence images of two day 5 trunk morphs show DAPI (grey), brightfield, BMP4:Achilles (green), and FOXF1:mScarlet3 (red), with BMP4 and FOXF1 reporter expression restricted to lateral domains. Images are representative of 4 independent experiments (13 chips, 36 trunk morphs) with similar results. f, Time series plot shows FOXF1:mScarlet3 (RFP) signal in hPSCs following a 14 h BMP pulse (blue), a 19 h BMP pulse (red), or a 19 h BMP pulse followed by LDN treatment (green), from the same experiment as Fig. 5i (n = 4 image series per condition; thick line, mean across series; shaded area, s.e.m. across series; each series value is the mean over the 50–200 cells segmented in that frame). See main text and Methods for details. g, Bulk RNA-seq analysis of neuromesodermal progenitor (NMP) and lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) cells differentiated on magnetic beads show elevated expression of canonical fate markers relative to pluripotent stem cells. Each column represents an individual sample, rows correspond to key genes, and values indicate normalized gene expression as shown by the colour scale (n = 3 biologically independent replicates per condition). h, Epifluorescence images show a replicate day 5 trunk morph from the same chip as in Fig. 5k but without an LPM donor graft, displaying DAPI (grey), brightfield, host cells (scramble control sgRNA transduced, CFP+, yellow), MESP2:mCherry (red) and FOXF1:Achilles (cyan). Images are representative of 3 independent experiments with similar results. i, Brightfield images of host cyst (yellow arrowhead) aligned with magnet (top), and following injection of a donor cell-coated magnetic bead (arrow) at a defined position (red circle, bottom). Images are representative of 9 independent experiments with similar results. Scale bars, 100 µm.

a, A second example, as in Fig. 5j, shows brightfield and epifluorescence images of a magnetic bead (black arrow) coated with donor cells from the FOXF1-T2A-Achilles; MESP2-T2A-mCherry reporter hPSC line constitutively labelled with H2B-emiRFP (magenta). Donor cells were pre-differentiated for 2 days into LPM (FOXF1:Achilles+, cyan) and grafted onto naïve day 2 host morphs (FOXF1-T2A-Achilles; MESP2-T2A-mCherry reporter hPSC line, scramble control sgRNA transduced, CFP+, yellow) with no prior BMP exposure. Images are representative of 9 independent experiments with similar results. b, A second example, as in Fig. 5k, showing distinct domains of donor (magenta) and host (yellow) cells. Paraxial mesoderm and somites are marked by MESP2:mCherry (red). Donor LPM (H2B-emiRFP+, magenta; FOXF1:Achilles+, cyan) is adjacent to host LPM (CFP+, yellow; FOXF1:Achilles+, cyan) induced next to the donor cells (white arrow). Images are representative of 6 independent experiments with similar results. c, A second example, as in Fig. 5l, day 5 morph derived from a day 2 host morph differentiated without BMP signalling, following transplantation of a magnetic bead coated with donor LPM cells (H2B-emiRFP+, magenta; FOXF1:Achilles+, cyan). Adjacent to the donor LPM (H2B-emiRFP+, magenta; FOXF1:Achilles+, cyan), the host morph shows a FOXF1+ (Achilles+, cyan; H2B-emiRFP−) LPM, as well as PAX8+ (immunostained, yellow) intermediate mesodermal domains lateral to somitic tissue (MESP2:mCherry+, red). Images are representative of 2 independent experiments (2 trunk morphs) with similar results. d, As in c, with donor LPM (H2B-emiRFP+, FOXF1:Achilles+, magenta) transplanted onto a host morph. The host shows a FOXF1+ (Achilles+, cyan; H2B-emiRFP−) LPM, as well as WT1+ (immunostained, yellow) intermediate mesoderm domains lateral to somitic tissue (MESP2:mCherry+, red). WT1 was immunostained after quenching and imaged in a second round, aligned to the first round using DAPI (see Methods). Images are from one experiment (1 trunk morph). e, As in b, donor LPM (H2B-emiRFP+, FOXF1:Achilles+, magenta) transplanted onto host morph (CFP+) in the presence of BMP inhibitor, NOGGIN, does not induce FOXF1+ LPM in the host (absence of CFP+ H2B-emiRFP− FOXF1:Achilles+ cells). Images are representative of 4 independent experiments (5 chips) with similar results. f, As in Fig. 5m, donor LPM (H2B-emiRFP+, FOXF1:Achilles+, magenta) transplanted onto host morph with a BMPR1A knockdown (CFP+) does not induce FOXF1+ LPM in the host (absence of CFP+ H2B-emiRFP− FOXF1:Achilles+ cells). Images are representative of 4 independent experiments (14 trunk morphs) with similar results. Scale bars, 100 µm.

a, As in Fig. 5o, live time-series images of two NMP fusion experiments. Rows: Days 1, 2, 3, 4; Columns: Brightfield, host (scramble control sgRNA transduced, CFP+, yellow), donor NMP (H2B-emiRFP+, magenta) on a magnetic bead (black arrow), merged host/donor, and MESP2:mCherry (red). Donor NMP cells transplanted onto pluripotent cysts and maintained in basal medium drive axial elongation and formation of MESP2:mCherry+ somites. Images are representative of 2 independent experiments (5 trunk morphs) with similar results. Scale bars, 100 µm.

Tottenham star Savio is not expected to play again this year, dealing a major blow to Roberto De Zerbi’s attacking options during the busy festive period.

According to The Athletic, the 22-year-old is expected to spend several weeks on the sidelines after suffering a hamstring injury during last weekend’s 2-0 Premier League victory over Ipswich Town.

The news comes as a major blow to Roberto De Zerbi, whose side have won four of their last five Premier League matches following a difficult start to the campaign.

With Tottenham looking to build on their recent resurgence during the busy festive period, they could now be without one of their most expensive summer signings until the new year.

Savio came off the bench in the 63rd minute against Ipswich, making his first appearance since Tottenham’s 1-1 draw with Manchester United on October 10.

However, his return to action lasted little more than 20 minutes before he went down inside the Ipswich penalty area following a solo run.

The Brazilian was visibly gutted, covering his face with his shirt as Tottenham’s medical staff helped him off the pitch. He was subsequently replaced by Archie Gray in the 89th minute.

While an exact recovery timeline has yet to be established, The Athletic reports that there are fears Savio could miss all seven of Tottenham’s remaining matches in 2026.

Those fixtures include Sunday’s trip to Sunderland and crucial December encounters against Arsenal and Liverpool.

Savio had only just recovered from a muscle injury that had forced him to miss four Premier League matches, making his latest setback particularly frustrating.

Arriving from Manchester City in August in a blockbuster transfer worth up to £85 million, Savio came to North London carrying big expectations to spearhead De Zerbi’s frontline.

Despite making an instant impression by scoring and assisting on his debut in a 5–1 Carabao Cup win over Charlton Athletic, persistent fitness setbacks have restricted him to just seven appearances across all competitions.

In his absence, teenager Luca Williams-Barnett is poised for extended minutes.

The youngster impressed on his first league start, scoring and assisting vs Ipswich to help Spurs win 2-0.

#1239. Premier League Goal of the Season 2026/27 Power Rankings

The Premier League is here for 2026/27 and over £3 billion spent in the summer, there is more firepower than ever in the world's most watched league.

Years gone by have seen some of the craziest goal compilations for completed seasons and the 2026/27 campaign has already provided its share of action as fans continue to feast on an incredible lineup of players and moments.

Here, GIVEMESPORT is tracking the best goals as and when they hit the net, ranking them in order based on a number of factors, which you can see below — culminating in our goal of the season pick come May, with the best strikes worldwide tracked in our Puskas Award power rankings. Here's how it stands.

There's something about Cole Palmer and Brighton: he loves playing against the Seagulls. It might be because they play the type of free-flowing football that allows him to score solo efforts like this one in their 4-3 victory in the opening weeks of the new season.

Palmer picked up the ball deep in Brighton's half and eyed the space ahead to the left to drive into. He took a few defenders along for the ride, showing quality dribbling, close control and pace, before applying a classy, curled finish to settle the game. Classic Palmer.

We've seen Bryan Mbeumo score plenty of clinical efforts during his time in the Premier League, and this opener against Everton shows that he is still improving. The poise, the quality and the ruthlessness at which he netted this ensure it ranks high on the list.

After receiving the ball on the right wing, he opted to move inside, hurrying the Everton defenders and midfielders, driving into the open space and firing a powerful low strike that left Jordan Pickford, one of the league's best goalkeepers, stranded.

This list is great because it currently holds a lot of variety, and Nilson Angulo brings a quality free-kick to the table here. He joined Sunderland in February but not many people know of the young attacker.

That changed in an instant as he produced a stunning free-kick from distance that cannoned in against Ipswich Town. Unfortunately, it was in vain, as the home side grabbed a key victory. Yet, the strike remains beautiful and likely remain on this list until another set-piece goal can top it.

This is a stereotypical 'great' goal. Harvey Barnes has proven over the years that he can produce big moments and powerful strikes with either foot — but this strike against Bournemouth was one of his best.

With a defender for company on the left, he quickly squared him up, cut inside and then fired a curling strike that nestled just inside the post. Virtually unstoppable, it deserves plenty of credit.

In what was the first match since City's guilty verdict, the occasion of Liverpool vs Manchester City at Anfield took on a whole new atmosphere — but Enzo Maresca's side revelled in the jeers to sweep aside their rivals by a comfortable 3-0 scoreline.

A red card for Ryan Gravenberch ensured City had the upper hand, and goals from Erling Haaland and Jérémy Doku had seen them take an unassailable lead. Then, City's wizard Rayan Cherki added the finishing touch with their third.

Cherki dummied Elliot Anderson's pass into the box, and then spun in behind to take the layoff from Joško Gvardiol. He controlled the ball, cut back inside to sell the defender before rolling it in with ease. Classy and brutal, all at once.

Maresca's City have been entertaining this season, albeit some distance away from their all-dominating form we've come to know in the past decade. With Fulham arriving at the Etihad as underdogs, an early good ensured they led for around 40 minutes before summer signing Elliot Anderson popped up with this volley.

Following a corner that was cleared to the edge of the box, the former Nottingham Forest midfielder showcased an exceptional technique to control his powerful volley low and in, managing to avoid the crowd of players in the box, to bring his side level.

The Paraguayan attacker has been hailed for his technical brilliance, and briefly featured on this list due to an exceptional assist he managed for striker Emersonn in the early parts of the season. This time, it's all about Enciso himself.

Facing a difficult Hull City side away from home, Ipswich found themselves chasing the game, at 2-1 down. Enciso stepped up, beat two players, then shifted it onto his left and fired an incredible strike into the top corner with his weaker foot. He is certainly their main man and when it comes to fighting off relegation in the Premier League table, they'll need more quality like this from him.

Add this to the list of Premier League centre-backs who've fired in unstoppable efforts. Sven Botman, one of Newcastle United's most experienced figures, fired his side back into contention during their Monday Night clash with Coventry. However, whilst this did make it 2-1 at the time, they fell to a sorry 4-1 defeat.

Still, Botman carried the ball deep in Coventry's half before firing his left-footed strike that arrowed into the near-post top corner. It's the type of strike that stands the test of time. Powerful, accurate and unforgettable.

There seems to be a trend with the promoted sides this season: none of them are afraid to have a go from distance. If Coventry are to stay up, then goals from like from Tatsuhiro Sakamoto are exactly what they need to pull off an incredible escape from the drop.

Against Crystal Palace, and their new boss Thomas Frank, the Japan international managed his second strike from outside of the box in as many weeks.

In what was first a tough cross to control, he chested it down and then fired it in from distance powerfully, leaving Dean Henderson with absolutely no chance.

Brighton has unearthed another gem in Diego Gomez. In an era where ball-striking from distance is less of a commonplace tactic, the young attacker is changing the status quo, as this strike marked his second entry on the list.

Facing another of the league's rising teams in Brentford, Gomez took it upon himself to settle a tight game, showcasing his quality with a fearsome weaker foot strike from outside the box. Not only is the strike quality, his cute little touches before firing it in on the half-volley, on the swivel by the way, is just pure technical brilliance. Something tells me he's going to feature on here again in the future.

#1238. Celtic Must Bite Bullet And Sack O'Neill - 'Elite' Manager Is Right There

Celtic need to bite the bullet and sack Martin O'Neill, despite their victory in the Europa League on Thursday night.

Celtic opened the scoring in the first half thanks to an own goal, but Portuguese side Torreense equalised just 10 minutes later.

Celtic were then held until the last five minutes of normal time, when Camilo Duran fired home to give Celtic the victory.

The Glasgow club have been picking up some strong results of late, but it's games that they are more than expected to win.

Their performances in the Europa League are where they will truly be judged, and in reality, it was another disappointing performance against Torreense.

They currently sit outside of the qualification section of the Europa League and look destined to be knocked out unless they beat Omonia Nicosia and other results go their way.

In the Scottish Premiership, Celtic are sitting top of the table by a single point, but given that's where they are expected to be, it's in Europe where they will be properly judged.

Celtic's performances in Europe this season simply haven't been good enough, despite two wins on the bounce in the competition.

Celtic made incredibly hard work of their win over Torreense, especially given the stature of the aforementioned club.

Torreense currently sit 13th out of 18 in the second division of Portugal. If Celtic are unable to get a convincing win against a side like that, it's worrying signs for O'Neill.

Given his age and his contract situation, everyone knows that O'Neill isn't going to be around Celtic for much longer, so why not bite the bullet and make a move?

They stand a serious chance of being knocked out of the Europa League, which would be a major disappointment considering the quality of some of the sides in there.

As mentioned, their Scottish Premiership form has been good of late, but it's still far from how O'Neill should be judged.

The Bhoys need to unlock their £6million signing

If Celtic are serious about trying to take the next step forward as a club, rather than having an ageing manager who is destined to leave, they need to go all out for former Ipswich Town manager Kieran McKenna.

He's currently out of work after leaving Ipswich, and although he may be waiting for better offers, it's certainly worth an ask.

McKenna, described as an 'elite' manager, isn't going to be a free agent for too much longer, so Celtic need to bite the bullet and make their move.

Whether they can attract him is another story, but there's no reason not to show some ambition if they want to take the next step.
