#1070. Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future

Germany's fall from grace in recent years has seen the team drift away from the fans. But Monday's drubbing of the Netherlands and the impact of Jürgen Klopp, Florian Wirtz and emerging youngsters offers hope.

"Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.

Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.

"Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.

"Instead, they'll be thinking: 'This could really turn into something. We have wonderful footballers, great characters," Klopp said, and added: "The lads are even surprising themselves."

The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach took the job in July after Julian Nagelsmann paid the price for another German early World Cup exit, this time to Paraguay in the last 32. Klopp always preached patience, particularly after his first two matches yielded a fortunate 1-1 draw with the Netherlands and a 1-0 home loss to Greece.

It paid off on Monday as Germany performed with the hallmarks of Klopp's great club sides — fierce pressing, intensity, pace and a measure of joy. Perhaps it is in Florian Wirtz that Klopp's impact is more notable.

The 23-year-old has struggled to make a significant impact at Liverpool since moving to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen at the beginning of last season. But he has four goals in his last four games for Germany and is demonstrating the ability that earned him a €125 million ($137.5 million) move to England.

"I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer," Klopp said after the Netherlands match.

"We've also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he's so vocal. He's the first pressing player, he can press two players without getting tired."

That quality was evident in Wirtz's first goal on Monday, when he won back possession on the edge of the Dutch box before combining some dazzling footwork with a brilliant, curled finish.

But Wirtz wasn't the only attacking bright spot for Germany. Rookie wingers Derry Scherhant and Brajan Gruda both scored and were a huge threat throughout. Klopp gave debuts to both earlier this year as he sought to spread opportunities. The pair have offered Germany a pace they often lacked under Naglesmann and his predecessor Hansi Flick.

"They can both play, my goodness," said Klopp.

Scherhant, who opened the scoring with another stunning strike, spent many days of his boyhood on the terraces of the Olympiastadion in Berlin, where Monday's game was played. Unlike many pros, he bounced about Berlin's lower league clubs as a youth before Hertha Berlin signed him up. He then moved to Freiburg in 2025 and is rapidly emerging as a player who can implement Klopp's style and reflect the coach's attitude.

"A few years ago, people told me I wouldn't make it as a pro. Then I became a pro. And even then, some people still said it wasn't enough—that the Regionalliga (Germany's fourth tier) was the best I could hope for,” Scherhant said.

"It's just unbelievable that I get to stand here now with the satisfaction of having proven those people wrong."

Proving people wrong is also a major part of Klopp's remit. After failing to get beyond the quarterfinal of a major tournament since 2016, the German public's interest in and enthusiasm for its men's national team had waned. Klopp's mission he said, was to "to prove to Germany and the world that we can play soccer."

While that was achieved on Monday, the loss (and subsequent 0-0 draw) against Greece in the Nations League game were evidence that it won't all be plain sailing. Indeed, Germany have had plenty of false dawns of late, as captain Joshua Kimmich alluded to.

"We've been through a tough time," he said. "A clear victory doesn't make all that go away," he added before saying that the task was to "turn potential into quality and a team that's all about 'what ifs' into a team that's all about 'reality.' That's the art of it."

Klopp too, for all his hype, was keen not to get too far ahead of himself.

"We want to gradually solidify it. We're not done yet. We still have a few areas to work on. But I'm looking forward to our future — it's crazy what's still to come," he said.

In Nations League terms, that will be a matchup with world champions Spain, or Portugal or Belgium before qualifying for Euro 2028 begins. For now though, Klopp and his players can enjoy some time with those smiles on their faces.

#1069. Welcome to Manchester United: Mauricio Pochettino faces grim reality after collapse against Liverpool

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

If he didn't already, Mauricio Pochettino knows what he has gotten himself into now. In his first press conference, the new head coach spoke of leading Manchester United to a "different place."

Oh, the places they might go if the first 15 minutes of Pochettino's tenure set the tone for the months ahead. Deepdale, Fratton Park, Ashton Gate. As United's defense buckled under Liverpool's ferocity, you really could convince yourself this was a team that might be at serious risk of relegation, a perpetual-motion machine turning bad vibes into worse performances. Losing to Liverpool away from home isn't a disaster; losing 4-0 after a 15th-minute red card is another matter entirely.

The table might have said otherwise, but there was not that much cause for anxiety when Michael Carrick was sacked and Pochettino appointed. For starters, they had appointed a coach with Premier League experience whose least successful postings over his coaching career have been the ones where he has delivered to expectations. That they did not go down the Igor Tudor route was probably enough to ensure United won't risk doing a Spurs.

The fixes seemed too straightforward: a better shape out of possession, cutting their diet of spray-and-pray shots. The analytics profile looked perfectly adequate at a stage of the season when expected goals is more predictive than goals and points. United were as near to dead average a Premier League team as you'd find. Eventually this would all have to bottom out.

And then Matthijs de Ligt started playing like a man who hadn't started a Premier League game in a year, moving like Jason Duval on his neighbor's mobility scooter. Leny Yoro made the mistake of a young center back who has been learning all the wrong habits, affording Alexander Isak just enough contact to allow him to go down and earn his team 82 minutes with a man advantage. Giving up a penalty and only getting a yellow might have been the better option for Yoro, even if it had allowed Isak to score another. The path the youngster took looked all the worse when Dominik Szoboszlai larruped in a free kick.

When Rio Ngumoha blew past Diogo Dalot and cut back for Florian Wirtz to acrobatically convert, it was game over. There was nothing for Pochettino to instill in this United team, nothing to be done but delay the inevitable shellacking.

Perhaps it speaks well of United's new coach that he swiftly understood his initial adjustment to the red card -- Patrick Dorgu dropping back to left back from the wing -- would be insufficient. On came Harry Maguire to marshal a back five. The bleeding was at least stemmed for a while before Ngumoha and Victor Munoz took the scoreline to 4-0 in the final 25 minutes. That that felt like a qualified success says everything about the humiliation United inflict on themselves when they rock up at Anfield.

United may be no wiser as to what Pochettino can do for them, but Pochettino will have a much clearer sense of how little some of these players can do for him. Lisandro Martinez was as cumbersome at left back as he has been in central defense this season, his limbs all at odds with each other as Bradley Barcola rushed by him to square for Ngumoha to score the third. He was not the only one eating dust when Liverpool got running. How could he be? The worst defensive record in Europe's top five leagues has to be a team effort.

Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo are no quicker in a Pochettino midfield than they were in Carrick's. De Ligt is going to need a long run of games to play himself back into form, but even then he does not have the athletic profile for a Premier League defender in the age of verticality. Nor do Dalot, Maguire, Martinez, Yoro, Noussair Mazraoui, Luke Shaw and Ayden Heaven. Perhaps there were moments at Anfield this afternoon where Pochettino found himself longing for Tim Ream, not for his composure and consistency, but for his burst across six yards.

He will have to get new defenders in January. Midfielders wouldn't go amiss either, even after all that cash that was splashed on Tielemans, Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos, who can safely assume he has left Pochettino quite unimpressed given that he was unused when United could really have used a ball-winning midfielder. "Don't worry about a thing," chanted those hardy few United fans who had waited out the final whistle. Come the end of the season, their optimism will probably be vindicated -- an average team that has appointed an above-average coach should be able to address a position less perilous than it seems. Every little thing should be all right. And yet there is a path ahead of United that really could take them to dark and dangerous places. Pochettino must now steer his club in another direction.

#1068. USA to co-host 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

FIFA confirmed its plans to stage the 2031 Women's World Cup in North America, with the joint bid from the U.S., Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica officially getting the green light at an extraordinary FIFA Congress in Zurich on Monday.

The announcement comes a year after the co-hosts formalized their commitment to put in a bid, one that was ultimately the only contender for the 2031 tournament. FIFA also confirmed its decision to host the 2035 Women's World Cup in the U.K.; that bid was also unopposed heading into Monday's meeting.

The Women's World Cup will return to North America for the first time since Canada hosted the tournament in 2015, while the U.S. will host the competition for the first time since 2003. Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica are all first-time hosts of the women's tournament, their inclusion in the bid part of an effort to accelerate the growth of women's soccer across the region. The 2031 World Cup, though, will also be another opportunity to showcase the growth of the women's game -- the U.S. has long been a hotbed for the sport, but its embrace of women's soccer has only grown since 2003, particularly with the increasing popularity of the uber-successful U.S. women's national team and the professionalization of the NWSL.

FIFA will return to the U.S. and Mexico fairly quickly after the two countries, alongside Canada, hosted the men's World Cup earlier this year, an experience that will prove to be relevant to the 2031 organizers from a logistical standpoint. Just as the men's World Cup did in 2026, the women's tournament will expand to 48 teams in 2031, a choice that ultimately resulted in the creation of a new competition footprint. U.S. Soccer president Cindy Parlow Cone said last year that the expansion was the main impetus for including Costa Rica and Jamaica in a bid that was once envisioned as a 32-team competition in just the U.S. and Mexico.

"As soon as I knew for sure that was in the works, I went to [Concacaf] president Victor Montagliani and talked to him about our vision and that we wanted to make it bigger and include more countries throughout Concacaf and wanted to work with him to pick which countries would be best suited," Parlow Cone said at the time. "Obviously, quality of teams, stadiums, infrastructure. Outside of stadiums, like hotels, training facilities also went into the decision."

Monday's announcement officially kicks off the process for a tournament FIFA hopes will attract more than 4.5 million spectators and estimates will generate more than $4 billion in revenue, which would make it the highest revenue-generating women's sporting event in history.

FIFA's bid evaluation report lists 20 stadiums that could host games, though the actual bid includes more than 30 cities and 45 venues that will vie for the chance to host games in 2031. Most of the 14 cities across the U.S. and Mexico that hosted the 2026 tournament are back in the mix, including the host of this year's final, MetLife Stadium in the New York area, and the semifinal venues of AT&T Stadium in the Dallas suburbs and Atlanta's Mercedes-Benz Stadium. A few cities that did not make the cut last time around, though, are also interested -- Denver's Empower Field is on the list, as is the under-construction stadium in Washington, D.C., that the NFL's Washington Commanders will call home and is expected to be complete in 2030.

The list of contenders in Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica is understandably smaller considering each country's size and the resources available. While competition to host games could heat up around North America, a fairly straightforward answer is expected in Jamaica. The under-renovation Independence Park in the capital city of Kingston is the only venue listed in the bid.

The 2031 bid is attracting more interest from potential host cities than the 2026 tournament did for one reason in particular -- tournament organizers are inviting bids from a wider range of stadiums this time around.

This year's men's World Cup was hosted exclusively in NFL stadiums or similarly sized venues in Canada and Mexico, some of which will likely stage games again in 2031 and welcome the teams that are expected to draw big audiences like the host teams in their home countries. There are a number of venues with a capacity of 40,000 seats or fewer, like Geodis Park in Nashville, Tenn., and San Diego's Snapdragon Stadium, that could make the cut in the end. Tournament organizers are entertaining the idea that strong atmospheres in smaller stadiums might be preferable to half-full venues for games that are not expected to welcome large audiences, though a final decision has yet to be made.

The vast majority of games are likely to be staged in the U.S., just as they were for the men's World Cup this year.

There is little concern about North America's ability to host the Women's World Cup as far as the economics go. The U.S. alone is as ideal a market as any for a women's sporting event and has been for decades -- around 14 million people in the U.S. watched the national team beat China in the final via an iconic penalty shootout in 1999, while that tournament generated a $4 million profit on its $30 million operating costs. The question for 2031, though, is who will actually make money.

The U.S. cities that hosted the men's World Cup this year spent the months before and after the tournament complaining about the economics, the local host committees footing bills that reportedly ran as high as $150 million per city to actually stage the tournament. The host committees at times successfully lobbied the Trump administration for federal funding, but they continued to express concerns about the division of costs between the cities and FIFA. The host committees were also reportedly waiting for a further $1 million weeks after the World Cup ended despite a pledge from FIFA president Gianni Infantino.

Potential host cities for the 2031 World Cup will likely advocate for a different split of the costs this time around, and the same could be true for the U.K.-set 2035 tournament. Local officials in the U.S. are reportedly contemplating banding together with the support of U.S. Soccer in the hopes of negotiating more favorable contracts with FIFA and avoiding fierce competition between the host cities that would strengthen FIFA's negotiating position.

#1067. Liverpool calamity hands Iraola his most chastening night yet

Andoni Iraola looked up to the ceiling of Fenerbahce’s media auditorium as he tried to find the words to describe the madness he had just witnessed.

“Cheap” was his first conclusion, swiftly followed by “messy”; technically, Liverpool’s head coach was right but this was a moment when nobody would have found issue had he gone further. “Absurd” and “preposterous” would have been more accurate portrayals of this calamity.

Liverpool have won two European trophies in Istanbul, but they do not tend to enjoy visits to Turkey. Roy Hodgson, in August 2010, was the last Anfield manager to oversee a win here and there was an irony that the hero of that night in Trabzon – Dirk Kuyt – masterminded this downfall.

Kuyt, interim head coach, got a remarkable response out of a Fenerbahce team who had amassed 1,086 Premier League appearances between them and he was as giddy as the locals after Mason Greenwood, Archie Brown and substitute Vedat Muriqi scored to give the club a famous night.

But even Kuyt would have been the first to recognise the helping hand Fenerbahce were afforded. Liverpool were meek, naïve, and while the Turkish side danced in the rain on the Asian side of the city, Iraola was left to dissect the most chastening 90 minutes of his short Anfield career.

“It’s frustration because it’s a difficult place to come here and to play,” said Iraola. “During most of the game, we were thinking: ‘OK we can win this one.’ But obviously it hasn’t happened. We conceded, I think, messy goals, especially the first and the third one. The second one is a rebound.”

Yet it all started so smoothly. For all that Fenerbahce tried to put Liverpool out of their stride with a soundtrack of high-pitched whistling, Iraola’s side kept the ball well and they might have been ahead in the fifth minute but Victor Muñoz and Bradley Barcola, playing as a central striker, erred.

Another chance went begging when Joe Gomez fizzed a ball across the six-yard box that was screaming to be converted, but nobody could apply the finishing touch. When Trey Nyoni put Liverpool ahead, it seemed like all those local predictions of a resounding away win would come true.

Nyoni is a terrific player-in-the-making and the joy of seeing him wheel away, having become Liverpool’s second youngest Champions League scorer behind Trent Alexander-Arnold, was everything you want to see in football.

So for the landscape to change so dramatically – and so quickly – after Liverpool had taken the lead was staggering, and it all came about after Irfan Can Kahveci slid in and turned a cross from Mattéo Guendouzi on to the bar.

Those who remember Kuyt from his Anfield days 15 years ago will recall a player who never considered any cause to be lost and the Dutchman implored his team to attack the flanks with pace, even earning himself a yellow card at one point. Eventually, the pressure paid off.

Greenwood had felt aggrieved not to have been given a 23rd-minute penalty, after Kostas Tsimikas placed his hands on his back, but he did not have to wait long to make an impact, his opportunity coming after Dominik Szoboszlai conceded a cheap free-kick.

Szoboszlai is rapidly becoming an enigma. How can a player with the gift of being able to score goals from the heavens make the mistakes of a weekend amateur? There was no need for him to foul N’Golo Kanté but the error was compounded, Greenwood’s strike deflecting off Jérémy Jacquet.

Since Manchester United felt duty-bound to sell Greenwood in 2024 the former England forward has continued his career away from the Premier League. After leaving Marseille he has found a home in Istanbul where the fans have taken to him and they bellowed his name following the equaliser.

Alisson Becker, wrong-footed by Jacquet’s decision to break off from the wall and turn his body, was livid and rightly so. Liverpool had gone from sublime (in patches) to ridiculous and the passage of play up to the interval was hugely uncomfortable.

Would things settle down after the break? Not a bit of it. Liverpool, worryingly for Iraola, could not stamp any authority and though there was a brief respite when Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak combined after being introduced as substitutes, the lead felt as sustainable as a snowball in a sauna.

Andoni Iraola says he will not waste any more time thinking about the penalty Liverpool were denied against Arsenal and won’t seek an explanation from Pro Ref. There was a significant fallout following the 1-0 loss at Anfield on Sunday with many judges believing Stuart Attwell, who was VAR, should have consulted match official Andy Madley to highlight an obvious pull by Jurrien Timber that prevented Alexander Isak heading a Bradley Barcola cross.

Liverpool have made the long trip to Turkey to take on Fenerbahce on matchday four of the Champions League.

Liverpool enter this fixture having won all three Champions League matches thus far, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal to make it nine points from nine for Andoni Iraola’s side. Liverpool’s five-game unbeaten streak was ended by Arsenal in the league on Sunday. They return to the city where the club enjoyed one of their most memorable nights, beating AC Milan in the Champions League final 21 years ago.

“Istanbul is always going to be very special for Liverpool,” Iraola said. “It is difficult to find a more important night. Tomorrow [tonight] it won’t be easy, you talk about statistics, especially English teams playing here. They have very good players and a very good squad, they know how to play in this competition. We have to start strong in the game. It is very early in the season to establish comparisons. We want to continue how we have done in the Champions League, three games and nine points, it is a good chance to get to 12 points and then finish in the top eight. Champions League away is very difficult.”

In addition to the long-term absentees Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Giovanni, both Ryan Gravenberch and Jeremie Frimpong have missed the trip to Turkey.

Fenerbahce have made a slow start to their Champions League campaign, taking just two points from their opening three fixtures. They have drawn twice against Roma and Slavia Prague at home whilst they suffered a heavy 6-0 loss at Aston Villa. Former Liverpool forward Dirk Kuyt has been appointed their interim coach following the resignation of Ismail Kartal following their recent defeat to arch rivals Galatasaray just over a week ago.

“It is a great opportunity for us to show what we can do,” Kuyt said. “It is also a great opportunity for me, a game between two teams that are very important to me. We have a very good plan, and we have to believe in this plan. No-one who loves Fenerbahce is happy with the current situation, but this is a huge opportunity. We have players who have won the Champions League and the World Cup.”

They come into tonight’s match having lost back-to-back league games since drawing against Slavia Prague on matchday three of the Champions League. They have plenty of former Premier League players in their ranks, including Ederson, N’Golo Kante and Romelu Lukaku.

#1066. Students' List candidates take seats as Serbian parliament opens

Serbia's Student List's candidates have taken their oaths in the inaugural parliament session. As the new majority, they have 90 days to form a government.

Representatives of Serbia's student-led movement were sworn in as lawmakers on Tuesday, just over four weeks after they ended Serbia's strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic's 14 years of rule.

The Students' List candidates officially took their seats in the inaugural parliamentary session as the first step for the youth-backed party toward forming Serbia's new government.

The movement holds 140 seats in the 250-member parliament while Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) holds 103. The remaining seats belong to ethnic minority parties.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hundreds gathered outside the parliament building in the capital Belgrade, to show their support for the student-backed lawmakers, most of whom are teachers, professors and other professionals with little or no political experience.

Meanwhile, SNS candidates were met with a negative reaction from the crowd. A woman in the crowd poured yogurt over an SNS member's head as she climbed the steps to the parliament entrance.

According to Serbian media, the newly elected lawmakers have been preparing for their first session for days. They will face veteran opposition politicians, including Aleksandar Vucic, who became the opposition leader after his defeat.

The Students' List will have 90 days to name a prime minister, present their programme and form a government, once the parliament is formed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The movement unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focused on making changes in domestic politics and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.

They pledged to improve healthcare, boost education and double the defense budget, along with many other reforms.

The election of a new parliamentary speaker will also lead to the appointment of a new acting president. The speaker has held the role since Vucic resigned in September to run for prime minister.

A snap presidential election must be called by November 27 and held by December 27.

Both parties are expected to put forward presidential candidates, but Vucic cannot seek another term because the constitution limits presidents to two terms in office.

#1065. Nvidia forms national security committee after Huang affair

Nvidia has created a board-level committee for national security and export control. This follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, allegedly including one with a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia on Tuesday said it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee.

This follows the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China and working to help ensure higher quality chips crucial to AI development made it to the Chinese market.

The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable company in the space of a month.

Since Huang's resignation, some investors — including Elon Musk and Donald Trump — have voiced concern that his departure could leave Nvidia and America's AI sector in peril and are now calling for his return. Huang on Tuesday, expressed regret for "serious mistakes" in his personal life before declaring he would be "honored" to return if the company's board of directors thought that was "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America."

Nvidia is calling the new group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.

Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair the committee, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).

The committee will meet at least once every quarter. It will also incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts.

Nvidia already has a lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team; these groups will report to the board-level committee.

"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Board Chair Harvey Jones said in a statement.

The company did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace, but the timing seemed conspicuous.

The decision was announced hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its still-stratospheric share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US President Donald Trump, whom Huang was influential in persuading to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other US companies and officials deemed prudent, welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday.

"Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great company," he said during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with the other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea."

Trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell. He also owns shares in other big tech companies.

Huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to Nvidia employees. This followed widespread reports, seemingly based on US and other intelligence, that one of the affairs was with a woman who used to lead a Singapore-based cloud computing company.

That company, Megaspseed International, is a major Nvidia client and is suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls. Intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.

The reporting on the case also seems to show these suspicions had been known to US officials and other countries, including Singapore, for roughly a year.

#1064. SFA are told to think again by clubs as latest youth plans are kicked into touch

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 13:49 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 14:19 EST, 26 November 2026

The SFA have been forced back to the drawing board for a second time in their efforts to introduce new proposals around youth development.

Led by chief football officer Craig Mulholland, the plans had been geared towards ensuring more Under-21 players in Scotland gain more minutes at first-team level.

The original plans were for two Scotland-eligible Under-21 players to start in domestic cup competitions, and for players to feature for a minimum of six per cent of all available minutes across a season in league campaigns.

When it became clear that several clubs in Scotland weren’t on board, a new watered-down version was put back on the table.

But the new proposals have also now been met with resistance — forcing the SFA to kick the can further down the road into the new year.

There will now be no vote on the back of the upcoming AGM, with further discussions required prior to something more concrete coming to fruition for the start of next season.

SFA chief football officer Craig Mulholland has been sent back to the drawing board by clubs

A statement from the governing body said: ‘The Scottish FA has been encouraged by the productive dialogue with clubs regarding proposals to harness opportunities for young homegrown talent.

‘The most recent discussions have spawned a range of additional potential innovations that all parties agree will require further consultation in order to present a consolidated package of recommendations to an SPFL member vote.

‘The passion we all have for Scottish football has been demonstrated by the public debate sparked since the all-club meeting in St Andrews, when the reality of our domestic game’s standing in respect of playing time for under-21 players compared to the rest of Europe was made clear.

‘We will continue to engage in dialogue with the aim of delivering a proposal that will achieve the stated objective of improving opportunities for young homegrown players to fulfil their potential at the top end of the Scottish professional game.

‘It is an objective everyone benefits from: players, clubs, supporters and Scotland national teams.

‘We have therefore agreed that the consultation process will continue into the New Year with the intention of a comprehensive proposal going to SPFL members within the first quarter of 2027, in time for the start of William Hill SPFL season 2027-28.

‘The Scottish FA General Meeting to vote on the complementary Scottish Gas Men’s Scottish Cup proposals will now follow a similar timetable.

‘Given the implications for our game, and our young talent, it is imperative that we take the necessary time to get those proposals right.’

#1063. Washington Spirit part ways with Adrian Gonzalez after loss in NWSL Championship

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Washington Spirit parted ways with head coach Adrian Gonzalez on Monday, less than 48 hours after a 2-1 loss to the Kansas City Current that marked the team's third successive defeat in the NWSL Championship.

Gonzalez was an assistant on the 2024 team that lost to the Orlando Pride in the final but he served as the interim before Jonatan Giraldez's midseason arrival from Barcelona. He then succeeded Giraldez after he left for France's OL Lyonnes, another club in Spirit owner Michele Kang's portfolio, midway through the 2025 campaign. He was a finalist for the NWSL's coach of the year award last season and maintained a consistency that has been a trademark for the Spirit in recent years, ensuring they continued to be serial contenders for titles under both Giraldez and Gonzalez.

For all their ambition, though, the Spirit have struggled to win major titles in the years since Kang took over the club in 2022. Their only title since is the 2025 Challenge Cup, a one-off game against the Pride, and have failed to win the NWSL Shield despite inching close on a handful of occasions while also falling short in the NWSL Championship games. They also failed to win the Concacaf W Champions Cup earlier this year, losing 5-3 to Club America in the final.

"I'm incredibly proud of what we've accomplished together at the Washington Spirit and grateful to the players, staff, ownership and supporters for their commitment and support throughout my time here," Gonzalez said in a club statement. "It has been an honor to lead this group, and I'm especially proud of the resilience and character the team has shown. A special thank you to the Spirit fans, who make this club truly unique. The connection and bond we've built with you has meant so much to me and made my time here even more special. Your passion and support are something I will always remember. While this chapter comes to an end, I'm excited for what lies ahead for the club and wish everyone continued success."

Gonzalez's departure also comes after Haley Carter became the president of soccer operations in the build-up to the 2026 season. Carter was previously with the Orlando Pride, who won both the NWSL Shield and NWSL Championship in 2024 after years of being a bottom-dweller in the league.

"We are grateful to Adrian for his leadership and the success he has helped bring to the Spirit over the past three seasons," Carter said in a statement. "He has led the team with class and professionalism and made a lasting contribution to this club. As we plan for the Spirit's future, all parties believe a change in leadership is necessary to build on that success and achieve our long-term sporting goals."

The search for Gonzalez's successor is underway and is likely to center around the Spirit's continuing quest to win the NWSL's top titles.

Since Kang's 2022 takeover, the ambitions of the Spirit have been clear as day. This is a team that is purpose-built to compete for titles, to the point that their attempts to keep Trinity Rodman in the NWSL led the league to create a brand-new rule and a historic contract for the player herself. The Spirit's entire roster, though, is impressive in its own right – Rodman counts Italy international Sofia Cantore amongst her partners in attack, while Tanzania's Clare Luvanga has scored four goals and notched three assists since her September arrival.

Gonzalez understood the assignment, even if the only accolade he walked away with was the 2025 Challenge Cup. He actually leaves the Spirit with 32 wins from 58 and a 1.84 points-per-game record, the best tally from a coach in the history of the NWSL. The strike on his record is that the Spirit did not rise to the occasion in the championship both last year and especially on Saturday, when a physical Current disrupted the momentum of the game and rattled the Spirit from start to finish. His will be a tough act to follow, though – he was able to get the best out of the players despite the stop-start nature of his responsibilities in the early stretch of his tenure and only confirmed that the Spirit are a club with high standards.

Considering the ambitions of the club, the coaching search will be an intriguing one. The Spirit are an attack-minded team and it would not be a surprise if a coach of that ilk lands the job, but Gonzalez's successor will ultimately be tasked with actually winning the titles that have eluded the club in recent years. Someone with a winning track record might be preferred and even if there are few obvious candidates, the Spirit likely have the pull – and the resources – to sign almost anyone they would like. It is not the only layer of uncertainty as the search begins – Carter has never hired a head coach during her years in NWSL front offices, joining the Pride after Seb Hines took the role and departing before his August departure.
